findings.issue_text: packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts:8 — P1 (96%): The shared sync branch returns a native `Response` while its declared `refreshFunction: () => any` preserves each provider SDK's incompatible return shape: `const response = await fetch(process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT, {`. Google immediately reads `res?.data` (Google CalendarService.ts:94), and HubSpot treats the result as a camelCase `HubspotToken` (Hubspot CalendarService.ts:177-202); with credential sync enabled both receive a `Response`, so Google dereferences undefined and HubSpot persists/uses undefined tokens. Advisory (wrong shape): a single credential-sync endpoint must normalize into a typed token DTO (or each adapter must explicitly decode and translate its response) before crossing the provider adapter boundary. Strongest rebuttal: most changed adapters already expect `Response`; that fails because the same helper is also used by SDK-returning adapters, so its `any` contract makes the integration behavior depend on the selected app rather than the advertised sync feature.

packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts:25 — P1 (91%): The minimal sync response parser invents a credential field instead of preserving the old value: `if (!refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token) { refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"; }`. Office365Calendar merges this parsed object over the persisted credentials (`{ ...o365AuthCredentials, ...tokenResponse.data }` at CalendarService.ts:264), so the documented sync response containing only an access token/expiry overwrites the real refresh token with the sentinel. That violates the credential state invariant and permanently leaves the record unable to do a provider-side refresh. Advisory (wrong shape): model sync results as a partial access-token update and merge only fields supplied by the sync service; delete the sentinel assignment. Strongest rebuttal: the sentinel may satisfy schemas that require `refresh_token`; it fails because it is persisted as an actual OAuth token and therefore corrupts the source-of-truth credential rather than merely satisfying an in-memory validation type.

packages/app-store/salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts:101 — P1 (94%): The newly refreshed Salesforce token is persisted but the live connection is constructed from the stale pre-refresh object: `accessToken: credentialKey.access_token,`. Every service construction first refreshes and writes `accessTokenParsed.data` (lines 75-99), then sends API calls with the old access token at line 106, so expired credentials still fail on the request that triggered refresh; when sync is enabled, the newly synced token is never used at all. The connection must be built from the merged refreshed credential (including the retained refresh token/instance URL), not `credentialKey`.

packages/app-store/salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts:75 — P1 (92%): The Salesforce refresh path bypasses the newly introduced credential-sync dispatch: `const response = await fetch("https://login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token", {`. With credential sharing and `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` enabled, Salesforce always refreshes directly against Salesforce and never supplies `calcomUserId`/`appSlug` to the parent application, so this changed integration is excluded from the OAuth credential-sync acceptance path.

packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts:15 — P1 (89%): The response-parser feature gate is not propagated from the sibling dispatch gate: `if (APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT) {`. `refreshOAuthTokens` additionally requires `userId` (`&& userId` at refreshOAuthTokens.ts:5) and therefore leaves team credentials on their provider refresh path, while this code nevertheless forces their provider response through the sync endpoint's minimal response contract. Team-owned Google, Office365, and Salesforce credentials consequently do not retain the ordinary provider-specific parsing behavior whenever sync is merely configured.

packages/app-store/googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:93 — P1 (96%): Google has no response-shape adapter for the sync endpoint contract: `const token = res?.data;`. The sync helper returns the native `fetch` `Response` described as containing only access token and expiry data, whereas the prior Google flow returned the Google client's response with a `.data` payload. The credential update therefore cannot consume the sync endpoint's token payload, leaving the Google sync integration incomplete.

packages/app-store/hubspot/lib/CalendarService.ts:177 — P1 (93%): HubSpot likewise has no mapping from the documented sync response (`access token and expiry date`) to HubSpot's required `HubspotToken` fields: `const hubspotRefreshToken: HubspotToken = await refreshOAuthTokens(`. The returned native `Response` is treated as a HubSpot SDK token and then `expiryDate`, `expiresIn`, and `accessToken` are read directly, so the credential-sync endpoint cannot provide a usable HubSpot refresh result.

packages/app-store/larkcalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:80 — P1 (90%): Lark's refresh path still requires Lark's nested provider response and a replacement refresh token: `const data = await handleLarkError<RefreshTokenResp>(resp, this.log);`. The shared endpoint is explicitly contracted to return only an access token and expiry date, but no conversion/default-preservation is added here; enabled sync therefore cannot satisfy Lark's `data.data.refresh_token`, `refresh_expires_in`, and `expires_in` requirements.

packages/app-store/office365video/lib/VideoApiAdapter.ts:82 — P1 (88%): The Teams adapter discards the sync endpoint's stated expiry-date response field: `responseBody.expiry_date = Math.round(Date.now() + (responseBody?.expires_in || 0) * 1000);`. A sync response with an expiry date but no provider `expires_in` is overwritten with the current time, so every use remains expired and repeatedly re-enters credential refresh instead of honoring the synchronized expiry.

packages/app-store/webex/lib/VideoApiAdapter.ts:90 — P1 (91%): Webex has no compatibility path for the shared endpoint's minimal token response: `const parsedToken = webexRefreshedTokenSchema.safeParse(responseBody);`. Its mandatory schema requires provider-specific `scope`, `token_type`, `refresh_token`, and `refresh_token_expires_in`, despite sync being documented to return only access token and expiry; synchronization therefore cannot serve Webex credentials.

packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts:3 — P2 (86%): No automated tests were added for the new feature's essential enabled/disabled, user/team, and per-provider response-contract branches: `const refreshOAuthTokens = async (refreshFunction: () => any, appSlug: string, userId: number | null) => {`. The diff adds no test/spec files, leaving the divergent sibling gates and incompatible response serialization paths above without acceptance verification.

P1 (confidence 99) packages/app-store/googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:97 — `const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(googleCredentials, googleCredentialSchema);` stores the SafeParse result object (`{ success: true, data: ... }`) rather than its `.data`, whereas this field previously stored the credential payload itself. On the first externally synced Google refresh the persisted credential no longer has top-level `refresh_token`/`expiry_date`; the next request fails at `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)`, orphaning every affected existing Google integration until manually reconnected. This survives the happy-path refresh because the in-memory `googleCredentials` still works for that request.

P1 (confidence 97) packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts:26 — `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token";` fabricates and returns a replacement refresh token whenever the sync response supplies the documented access token/expiry only. In the Office365 calendar flow, the caller merges this parsed data into the stored key, so it overwrites the real refresh token with the literal string; disabling sync, a sync outage/fallback, or later migration back to provider refresh makes the credential permanently unrefreshable. Retaining the existing refresh token at the caller cannot rebut this because the spread at `office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:264` applies the fabricated value last.

P1 (confidence 96) packages/app-store/hubspot/lib/CalendarService.ts:177 — `const hubspotRefreshToken: HubspotToken = await refreshOAuthTokens(...)` treats the credential-sync `fetch` result as HubSpot's decoded `HubspotToken`. With sync enabled it is a `Response`, so `expiresIn` and `accessToken` are undefined; the subsequent persistence/use either fails JSON serialization or writes an invalid token payload and leaves the installed integration unable to refresh. The type assertion does not transform the response, and this path is only exercised during the migration/sync configuration.

P1 (confidence 91) apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts:62 — `const appCredential = await prisma.credential.findFirst({` implements a read-then-create sync without a unique constraint or transaction. Concurrent retry/delivery of an initial credential sync can both see no row and create duplicates; later reruns update one arbitrary `findFirst` row while the others retain stale credentials. This leaves ambiguous, orphaned credential state and is not mitigated by retries—the retry is precisely what creates/maintains the drift.

packages/app-store/salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts:96 — P1 (confidence 100): `await prisma.credential.update({` references `prisma`, but this module has no `@calcom/prisma` import; TypeScript reports `Cannot find name 'prisma'`, so the app-store build cannot compile.

P1 (99%) packages/app-store/googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:97 — `const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(googleCredentials, googleCredentialSchema);` returns Zod's `{ success: true, data }` wrapper, but line 100 persists that wrapper as `credential.key`; the next Google calendar construction calls `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` against `{success,data}` rather than token fields, so the first successful refresh corrupts the stored credential and all later Google calendar operations fail to initialize.

P1 (98%) packages/app-store/googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:94 — `const token = res?.data;` assumes the Google client/Gaxios response shape, while the enabled sync branch in `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a Fetch `Response` (`return response`); `token` is therefore undefined and `token.access_token` throws on every expired synced Google credential. The catch silently returns the old expired auth object (`if (message !== "invalid_grant") return myGoogleAuth`), so refresh never reaches the sync service and the subsequent calendar request fails with the stale token.

P1 (96%) packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts:8 — `await fetch(process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT, {` has neither an AbortSignal nor any deadline. Every expired user credential blocks a booking/calendar request on this new remote dependency indefinitely when the configured sync endpoint accepts a connection but stalls; upstream request timeouts then turn a transient sync outage into hung/failed booking work rather than a bounded integration failure.

P1 (94%) packages/app-store/larkcalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:84 — `const data = await handleLarkError<RefreshTokenResp>(resp, this.log);` parses the sync endpoint response as Lark's provider envelope and immediately dereferences `data.data.refresh_expires_in` (line 87), although the shared sync helper documents that its response contains only an access token and expiry. Thus an enabled credential-sync response cannot refresh Lark credentials: it lacks the nested `data`, replacement refresh token, and refresh expiry required here, causing the refresh path to throw and bookings using an expired Lark token to fail.

P2 (90%) packages/app-store/salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts:75 — the new unconditional token POST refreshes Salesforce on every `getClient` invocation, but the connection at lines 105-107 is still constructed from `credentialKey.access_token`/`refresh_token`, not `accessTokenParsed.data`. An expired credential therefore performs a refresh and database write yet makes the current event operation with the stale token (triggering a second jsforce refresh/401 path); even valid credentials incur an unnecessary remote refresh, increasing latency and provider throttling risk.

P2 (95%) apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts:31 — `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` and the later `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` (lines 57-59) are uncaught in this API handler. Malformed webhook JSON, invalid ciphertext, or a wrong encryption key becomes a framework 500 instead of a contract 4xx; ordinary sender/configuration mistakes are consequently retried as server failures and can repeatedly delay credential convergence.

packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/createOAuthAppCredential.ts:37 — P1 (94%): A user merely needs to be an accepted member to create a team-scoped OAuth credential: `userId: req.session?.user.id,`. The `teamId` is parsed directly from the caller-controlled, unsigned OAuth `state` (decodeOAuthState.ts:9), and this branch never calls the admin authorization helper used for user/no-team credentials. A non-admin member can start an OAuth flow with a forged `state.teamId`, complete it against an attacker-controlled provider account, and install that account's credential for the entire team; for example this permits redirecting a team's Stripe integration to the member's Stripe account or replacing its shared calendar/video integration.

goldens.comment: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.

The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.

parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse result ({ success, data, error }), not the credential key object. Persisting that as key stores the wrapper instead of the token payload; we should store the parsed data or use schema parse.

When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the refreshFunction helper returns the fetch Response, but several callers (for example GoogleCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting res.data, and HubspotCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting a HubspotToken) assume it returns the integration-specific token object. That mismatch will cause runtime errors in the sync-enabled path unless the return type or those call sites are adjusted.

When the sync endpoint path is used, res is a fetch Response and has no .data; res?.data will be undefined and token.access_token will throw at runtime. This relies on a consistent return shape from refreshOAuthTokens, which isn’t guaranteed currently.

The `refreshOAuthTokens` function is passed `credentialId` instead of `userId`, which breaks the credential sync functionality by causing incorrect user lookups. This issue can lead to failures in syncing user credentials, impacting user experience.

The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.

The `jsforce.Connection` is created using stale `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` after a token refresh, which can lead to authentication failures and incorrect data access. Ensure that the connection is established using the refreshed token values instead.

The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.

adjudication.rationale: The finding is accurate. Looking at the diff for packages/app-store/salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts (lines 72-91), the Salesforce integration adds a direct fetch call to 'https://login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token' for token refresh, but unlike other integrations modified in this PR (Google Calendar, HubSpot, Lark, Office365, Webex, Zoho, Zoom), it does NOT wrap this call with the new `refreshOAuthTokens()` function. Other integrations like Google Calendar (line 83-92), Office365 (lines 243-260), and Zoom (lines 76-97) all use `refreshOAuthTokens()` to conditionally route through the credential sync endpoint when APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is true.
